types.name: EScanResponse
types.doc:
What the surface does to the pulse that struck it. Every ray passes through
this, which is the whole reason the enum exists: a creature that eats the
scanner, one that throws a false wall, one that answers late and one that
answers everywhere at once are four table entries, not four special cases
wired into whatever draws the point cloud.

members.name: Return
members.doc: The point comes back where the ray struck.

members.name: Absorb
members.doc: Nothing comes back. The surface is a hole in the world.

members.name: Displace
members.doc: The point comes back, somewhere it was not.

members.name: Jitter
members.doc: The point comes back smeared around the true hit.

members.name: Penetrate
members.doc: The surface yields nothing and the ray carries on behind it.

members.name: displacement
members.doc: Displace: world-space offset applied to the reported position.

members.name: jitterRadius
members.doc: Jitter: radius in metres of the deterministic smear.

members.name: delaySeconds
members.doc: Delay: seconds the caller should hold the point for.

members.name: penetrateOffset
members.doc:
Penetrate: how far past the surface the ray resumes. Too small and the
continuation re-hits the same triangle; too large and it tunnels
through whatever is immediately behind it.

members.name: reportAs
members.doc:
The tag the emitted point claims. kScanTagInherit keeps the real one —
anything else is the surface lying about what it is.

types.name: FScanResponseTable
types.doc:
Tag rules describe materials; instance rules describe one actor. A creature
manipulating a player's scanner installs an instance rule and removes it
again, and never has to invent a material to do it.

Resolve() is const and lock-free by construction: a pulse reads the table
from every worker at once, so mutate it between pulses, never during one.

types.name: FScanPoint
types.doc:
One emitted sample. At most one per ray: a pulse is thousands of rays and
the output array is sized up front from the ray count, so nothing in the
cast loop allocates, locks, or merges per-thread buffers. Penetrate
therefore yields nothing at the surface it passes through — if a pierced
surface ever needs its own faint return, the cheap answer is a second ray,
not a variable-length output per ray.

members.name: delaySeconds
members.doc:
Non-zero only for Delay. The seam does not own a clock; the caller
holds the point for this long.

types.name: FScanResponseEvaluator
types.doc:
The single place a response is turned into a point, so that every ray in
the engine — the Embree scan hierarchy's and the existing Jolt batch
path's alike — goes through the same six branches. Whichever backend
produced the FScanHit, the behaviour downstream is identical, and adding a
seventh response is one edit rather than one per backend.

members.name: Apply
members.signature: static EOutcome Apply(const FScanResponseTable& table, const FScanHit& hit, uint64_t seed, uint32_t rayIndex, uint32_t penetrationsSoFar, FScanPoint& outPoint, float& outResumeDistance)
members.doc:
rayIndex and seed only feed Jitter, and they feed it through a hash so
that a pulse replayed anywhere produces the same cloud.

members.name: JitterOffset
members.signature: static Vec3 JitterOffset(uint64_t seed, uint32_t rayIndex, float radius)

members.name: Drop
members.doc: The surface ate the pulse; emit nothing.

members.name: Continue
members.doc: Penetrate: cast again from outResumeDistance and ask once more.

types.name: EScanLayer
types.doc:
Ray-mask bits. Segregating the world from the props from the characters is
what lets one pulse ignore a layer for the cost of an AND per test, instead
of a second BVH or a post-filter over the whole cloud.

types.name: FScanMeshData
types.doc:
Triangle soup plus one tag per triangle. Whatever produces it — the sector
collision proxy, a navmesh snapshot, a hand-authored scan mesh — hands the
seam this and nothing else.

members.name: triangleTags
members.doc:
Empty means "every triangle is uniformTag". Otherwise one entry per
triangle, i.e. indices.size() / 3.

types.name: FScanCapsule
types.doc:
A character proxy. Axis is +Y in the capsule's own space; the instance
transform puts it where the animation says the body is.

members.name: segments
members.doc:
Tessellation of the generated proxy mesh. The default is a body-sized
silhouette at scan range; raising it costs triangles in a BVH that is
rebuilt every frame.

types.name: FScanHit
types.doc:
What a backend hands the response table. Any backend: the Embree scan
hierarchy fills it from an RTCRayHit, and the existing Jolt batch path can
fill it from an FQueryHit. Nothing in here names a ray tracer, which is
what lets one response table sit over both.

members.name: normal
members.doc:
Already flipped toward the ray: a scanner standing inside a room hits
the back of every wall, and a normal pointing away from it is useless
to everything downstream.

free.name: FScanTag
free.doc:
What a surface answers to a scan pulse. Deliberately not ESurfaceType:
physics surfaces answer "what does a footstep sound like here", and a
scanner asks "what comes back off this" — a creature that reports itself
as stone must be able to lie about the second without touching the first.

free.name: kScanTagInherit
free.doc: On an instance, "keep whatever the part's triangles say".
